subject: civil
audience: FE Civil candidates and civil engineering students
title: The Pipe That Halved Its Diameter and Quadrupled Its Velocity
featured_title: THE PIPE THAT HALVED ITS DIAMETER AND QUADRUPLED ITS VELOCITY

presentation.challenge: The diameter fell by half. The velocity did not merely double—it rose from 1.5 to 6.0 m/s.

practice.primary_question: Why does halving a circular pipe diameter make velocity four times larger for the same incompressible flow rate?
practice.typical_exam_trap: Assuming velocity changes inversely with diameter instead of inversely with cross-sectional area.

case_dna.target_misconception: If pipe diameter is halved at constant flow rate, velocity only doubles.
case_dna.why_plausible: The inverse relation between flow area and velocity is remembered, but area is mistakenly treated as proportional to diameter rather than diameter squared.
case_dna.contradicting_evidence: Circular area is proportional to D². Reducing D from 0.20 m to 0.10 m reduces area to one-quarter, so V rises from 1.5 to 6.0 m/s.
case_dna.corrected_model: For steady incompressible flow, Q=A V. In a circular pipe, A=pi D²/4, so velocity is inversely proportional to D² at fixed Q.

problem_statement: Water flows steadily through a 200 mm diameter pipe at 1.5 m/s and then enters a 100 mm diameter section. A note predicts the downstream velocity is 3.0 m/s because the diameter is halved. Calculate the actual downstream velocity and identify the area-scaling error.

gates.label: Incident
gates.heading: The diameter halved. The velocity increased fourfold.
gates.prompt: Which geometric quantity—not diameter alone—controls continuity?

options.label: Use A1V1=A2V2 and A proportional to D squared
options.reason: Steady incompressible volumetric flow rate is conserved.

options.label: Use D1V1=D2V2
options.reason: Flow rate depends on area, not diameter.

options.label: Velocity stays constant because mass is conserved
options.reason: Mass conservation requires area and velocity to adjust together.

gates.label: Experiment
gates.heading: Measure the downstream speed
gates.result: Velocity in the 100 mm section is 6.0 m/s.

gates.label: Gap
gates.heading: Prove the velocity ratio
gates.hint: The diameter ratio must be squared.

gates.label: Evidence
gates.heading: Area scaling explains the fourfold increase

gates.label: Redline
gates.heading: Correct the continuity note
report: C1. Pipe diameter decreases from 200 mm to 100 mm.
C2. The flow rate remains constant.
C3. Therefore velocity only doubles from 1.5 to 3.0 m/s.

claims.label: C2
claims.reason: Steady incompressible flow conserves volumetric flow rate.

claims.label: C3
claims.reason: It ignores that circular area varies with diameter squared.

correction.template: The downstream velocity is {velocity} m/s because the area is one-quarter as large.

gates.label: Design Fix
gates.heading: Keep downstream velocity at or below 3 m/s
gates.constraint: Keep the same flow rate and upstream condition.

options.label: Use a downstream diameter of at least about 141 mm
options.reason: To limit V2/V1 to 2, area can halve, so diameter must be D1/sqrt(2)≈0.141 m.

gates.label: Transfer
gates.heading: Apply continuity
gates.prompt: At constant flow rate, if circular-pipe diameter doubles, velocity becomes what fraction of its original value?

options.label: One-quarter
options.reason: Area increases by four, so velocity falls by four.

options.label: One-half
options.reason: That treats area as proportional to diameter.

options.label: Unchanged
options.reason: Continuity requires velocity to change when area changes.

gates.explanation: At fixed Q, V is inversely proportional to D squared for a circular pipe.

gates.label: Sign Off
gates.heading: Sign off the continuity calculation
gates.confirmation: I confirm that pipe velocity changes with cross-sectional area, not linearly with diameter.

items.label: What failed
items.value: Velocity was scaled inversely with diameter rather than area.

items.label: What was missed
items.value: Circular area varies with D squared.

items.label: Corrected model
items.value: Use A1V1=A2V2 for steady incompressible flow.

seo.seo_title: Continuity Equation: Halving Diameter Makes Velocity 4× | FE Civil E-048
seo.meta_description: Solve FE Civil Case E-048: water at 1.5 m/s in a 200 mm pipe accelerates to 6.0 m/s in a 100 mm pipe.
seo.focus_keyphrase: FE Civil continuity equation pipe velocity
seo.excerpt: Halving pipe diameter reduces area to one-quarter, so constant-flow velocity becomes four times larger.
seo.direct_answer: For steady incompressible flow, A1V1=A2V2. Because circular area is proportional to D², reducing diameter from 0.20 m to 0.10 m reduces area by four. Therefore velocity rises from 1.5 m/s to 6.0 m/s.

faqs.q: What happens to velocity if pipe diameter is halved at constant flow?
Why not just use the diameter ratio?
faqs.a: Continuity uses cross-sectional area, and circular area is proportional to diameter squared.
